description: God as benevolent, omnipotent and eternal; the Trinity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
content_html:
What Do Christians Believe About God?

Christianity is a monotheistic religion — Christians believe there is only one God. Yet describing who that God is requires several key terms. Each attribute shapes how Christians think about God, how they pray, and how they live. The specification asks you to know these terms and what they mean for Christian life and worship.

The Attributes of God

Christians believe God is benevolent — all-loving and wholly good. This means God cares for every person and acts in love. It connects closely to the Christian understanding of God as a forgiving father who desires a relationship with humanity.

God is also omnipotent — unlimited in power. Christians believe God created the universe from nothing and sustains it. Jesus taught in Matthew 5:48, “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect” — a verse pointing to God’s total moral excellence. The idea of omnipotence is tied to trust: if God is all-powerful, Christians believe he can act in the world through miracles and answered prayer.

God is omniscient, knowing all things past, present and future. For many Christians this is reassuring: nothing is hidden from God, and nothing can surprise him. It also raises questions about free will, since if God knows what humans will do, in what sense are they truly free?

God is described as eternal — without beginning or end, existing outside time. He is also transcendent, existing beyond and outside the created world, and immanent, present within creation and personally involved with people. Christians hold both truths together: God is far above humanity, yet close enough to hear prayer. God is also understood as a judge — evaluating human behaviour — and as forgiving, offering a path back to relationship through repentance.

Key Fact

Key attributes Christians use to describe God: benevolent (all-loving), omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing), eternal (outside time), transcendent (beyond the world), immanent (present within the world), personal (in relationship with people) and forgiving.

The Trinity: One God, Three Persons

The most distinctive Christian belief about God is the Trinity. Christians do not believe in three gods; they believe in one God who exists in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This is expressed in the creeds of the Church and is central to Christian worship, baptism and prayer.

The term “Trinity” does not appear in the Bible, but Christians draw support from passages such as Matthew 6:9–15, where Jesus addresses God as “Our Father” in the Lord’s Prayer, and John 14:16–17, where Jesus promises the disciples that the Father will send “another advocate,” the Spirit of truth. The incarnation — God becoming human in Jesus — and the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost both contributed to the Church’s Trinitarian understanding.

Philippians 2:5–8 captures how Jesus, who was “in very nature God,” took on human form as a servant — a passage central to Christian thinking about the relationship between the Father and the Son.

Key Fact

The Trinity: God the Father (creator and sustainer), God the Son (Jesus, incarnate redeemer) and God the Holy Spirit (counsellor and guide). The doctrine was formally defined at the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE and is expressed in the Nicene Creed.

The Creeds and Sources of Authority

The Apostles’ Creed and the Nicene Creed are the principal statements of Christian belief. Both affirm belief in God the Father, Jesus Christ his Son, and the Holy Spirit. Most denominations — Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Methodist — use one or both in their worship.

Different denominations place different emphases on God’s attributes. Evangelical and Pentecostal Christians often stress God’s immanence — his closeness, availability and power to act in daily life. Catholic and Orthodox traditions tend to balance immanence with transcendence, using formal liturgy to express the distance and holiness of God as well as his nearness. Liberal Protestant Christians sometimes emphasise God’s benevolence and forgiveness, finding in the loving Father of the Lord’s Prayer the dominant image of God.

All mainstream denominations affirm the Trinity, though they may differ in how they explain the relationship between the three persons. Some traditions — particularly those influenced by Eastern Orthodoxy — prefer to describe the Trinity as three distinct persons who share one divine essence, while Western Christianity has sometimes begun from the unity of God and then explained how he is three.

Unitarians and Rejection of the Trinity

Not all who call themselves Christian accept the Trinity. Unitarian Christians, such as the Christadelphians, hold that God is strictly one person — the Father alone — and that Jesus was a fully human being, not divine. They argue that the doctrine of the Trinity was a later addition and is not found in scripture. This places them outside the mainstream of Christian teaching as defined by the historic creeds.

Belief in the Trinity shapes almost every area of Christian practice. Baptism is carried out “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” The Gloria (a liturgical doxology) praises all three persons. Many Christian prayers are addressed to the Father, through the Son, in the power of the Spirit. The Trinity also grounds the Christian understanding of love: because God is three persons in relationship within himself, love is not a later addition to God’s character — it is what he eternally is.

For Christians, knowing God as Trinity means prayer is never just speaking into the unknown. It is a relationship with a Father who knows them, a Son who shared their humanity, and a Spirit who lives within them.
exam_tip_html: When answering ‘Outline’ or ‘Describe’ questions on the Trinity, make sure you name all three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) and state that Christians believe in one God in three persons — not three separate gods. A common error is writing “Christians believe in three gods,” which is directly wrong. For the 15-mark ‘Discuss’ question on God’s attributes, use named sources such as the Nicene Creed, Matthew 5:48 or Matthew 6:9–15 to support your argument, and consider the Unitarian/Christadelphian counterpoint as a genuine alternative view. Accurate spelling of theological terms — benevolent, omniscient, omnipotent, transcendent, immanent — is rewarded in extended responses where SPaG marks apply.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians are monotheists who describe God using terms including benevolent, omnipotent, omniscient, eternal, transcendent, immanent, personal, judge and forgiving — each with significance for how they pray and live.
  • The Trinity is the belief that one God exists as three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), expressed in the Apostles’ Creed and Nicene Creed; it shapes baptism, prayer and worship across all mainstream denominations.
  • Unitarians such as the Christadelphians reject the Trinity and hold that God is strictly the Father alone, arguing Jesus was human rather than divine.

practice_questions.text: State what Christians mean when they describe God as omnipotent.
practice_questions.marks: God is all-powerful / God can do anything / God has unlimited power. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what Christians believe about God as both transcendent and immanent.
practice_questions.marks: Transcendent: God is beyond the created world, above and outside human experience. [1 mark] Immanent: God is present within the world and personally involved with human beings. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Christian belief in the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks from: the belief that one God exists as three persons [1]; named as Father, Son and Holy Spirit [1]; the persons are distinct but united in one divine being [1]; expressed in the Nicene Creed or Apostles' Creed [1].

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why belief in the Trinity is important for Christians.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- The Trinity shapes Christian worship and baptism, which is carried out in the name of all three persons. John 14:16-17 shows Jesus promising the Spirit as advocate, grounding Trinitarian belief in scripture. [up to 3 marks]
- The Trinity means God is eternally relational; because God is three persons in relationship, love is fundamental to his nature. Philippians 2:5-8 shows the Son willingly taking human form, expressing self-giving love within the Godhead. [up to 3 marks]
- Other valid points: the Trinity connects creation (Father), redemption (Son) and sanctification (Spirit); it shapes the Lord's Prayer (addressed to the Father) and the work of the Spirit in Christian lives. [3 marks per point: 1 for a simple statement, 2 for development, 3 for development with a named source]

practice_questions.text: 'Belief in the Trinity is the most important Christian belief about God.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- The Trinity is affirmed in both the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed, making it one of the most formally agreed Christian doctrines across denominations.
- It shapes every act of Christian worship: baptism, prayer, the Gloria and the structure of the Mass are all Trinitarian.
- Philippians 2:5-8 and John 14:16-17 provide biblical grounding for seeing the Son and Spirit as fully divine alongside the Father.
- Without the Trinity, the incarnation and atonement lose their significance: Jesus is only a saviour if he is fully divine.

Arguments against / alternative views:
- Unitarians such as the Christadelphians argue that strict monotheism — God as one person — is more important, and that the Trinity is a later human doctrine not found in scripture.
- Some Christians would argue that God's benevolence (love) is the most fundamental attribute, since without it the other attributes become frightening rather than reassuring.
- God's omnipotence might be seen as more foundational: if God is not all-powerful, then his promises, creation and salvation are all in doubt.
- Immanence may be more practically significant for many believers: the felt presence of God in daily life shapes behaviour and comfort more directly than doctrinal definitions.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Nicene Creed, Philippians 2:5-8, Unitarian position); explicit weighing of which belief is 'most important' with a justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides present with at least one named source; some comparison and a conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger than the other; limited sources; conclusion present but not fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; little or no use of sources; no real conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the Nicene Creed is used in Christian worship.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: said together at Sunday Mass / Anglican Communion service as a statement of shared faith [1]; used at baptisms to express the faith the candidate is entering [1]; used to unite Christians across denominations in affirming core Trinitarian belief [1]. [1 mark per valid point, max 2]

flashcard_questions.a: Transcendent = beyond the world; immanent = present within the world.

glossary_terms.definition: All-loving and perfectly good; God always acts in ways that are loving and kind.
All-powerful; God can do anything that is logically possible.
All-knowing; God knows everything, including the future and the innermost thoughts of every person.
Existing outside of and unaffected by time; without beginning or end.
Beyond human experience and completely separate from the physical world.
Present within the world and accessible to human beings.
The Christian belief that God exists as three persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — united in one divine being.
An early Christian statement of faith beginning 'I believe in God, the Father almighty', used in baptism and worship.
A creed produced at the Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and expanded in 381 CE, affirming the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ.
Christians who believe God is only one person, not three; they reject the full divinity of Jesus. The Christadelphians are one example.
